text: This lab is a worked scenario, not a click-through. You'll model a real three-tier web application entirely on paper, applying everything from this chapter: the CI test, the table hierarchy, and an honest eye on where data quality risk creeps in even at this small scale.

Harrow Logistics runs a customer-facing order tracking application, built the standard way: a web server for the public-facing site, an application server for business logic, and a database server holding order and customer data. Your job is to decide which cmdb_ci subclass fits each piece, and which class-specific fields each one would actually carry.

The application itself is a cmdb_ci_appl record, separate from any server — it carries version, vendor, and business criticality, and it passes Lesson 1's test cleanly since both its state and its dependencies genuinely matter. The web server and application server are each their own cmdb_ci_server record, with their own CPU, RAM, and operating system fields, because each has state that can change independently of the other.

The database tier is where the distinction from Lesson 2 really earns its keep. The database server, hosting the engine, is a cmdb_ci_server. The database instance itself, with its own schema and instance name, is a separate cmdb_ci_database record. The server can be patched and rebooted without the instance changing at all, and the instance can migrate to new hardware without its own schema changing — keeping them separate is what makes each one trackable on its own terms.

Even this simple, four-CI model is already exposed to Lesson 3's risks. If Discovery scans the servers automatically while the application record was entered by hand, their operational status could drift out of sync at different rates. And without a named owner for the application record, nobody is positioned to notice if its criticality or version falls out of date.

You've built one cmdb_ci_appl, two cmdb_ci_server, and one cmdb_ci_database record — four CIs that, right now, are disconnected. Nothing yet says the application runs on those servers, or that the app server talks to that database. That's exactly where Chapter 2 picks up: CI Relationships and Relationship Types, starting next lesson.
